name: Stretching machine (Height Increase)

card.summary: Traction or stretching devices that lengthen the spine for a short time, adding a few millimetres of measured height by decompressing the discs.
card.note: Marketed height gains are short-term disc effects; they do not lengthen bones.

quick.overview:
Stretching machines are benches, tables or frames that pull on or decompress the spine. People use them hoping to look and measure taller. The effect they work with is real: the discs between vertebrae lose water through the day and recover with rest, so measured height varies, and stretching can nudge posture and disc hydration.

They do not act on the growth plates or bones. One study found a child's height fell by an average of 1.5 cm between morning and late afternoon, and a randomised trial has examined postures designed to rehydrate discs and raise spinal height.
quick.how: Users lie or hang in the device for a session, often as part of a stretching routine alongside posture work. Any added height is typically measured soon after and reverts through the day. Surgical limb lengthening is a separate, much larger procedure.
quick.risks: Many devices are sold as back-pain tools. Reviewers on retail pages report mixed experiences, including one who felt an unsecured joint position caused injury. Traction is generally unsuited to people with certain spine or circulation conditions, so a clinician is usually consulted first.

lead: Stretching machines used for height are traction or decompression devices: benches, tables or frames that lengthen the spine by gravity, weight or mechanical pull. Retailers mostly market them for back pain, while people interested in height use them to chase a few extra millimetres.

How they connect to looks: the spine's intervertebral discs hold water, so measured height varies through the day. One study of 100 children found a mean decrease of 1.54 cm from rising to late afternoon, and lying down for a long time raises measured height.[3] A randomised trial has tested sitting postures aimed at rehydrating discs and increasing spinal height.[1] A machine aims at the same disc effect, plus better posture, and the result is a taller-looking, taller-measuring frame for a period of time.

Growth ends at around age 15-16 for average females and 18-19 for average males, and the machines are not designed to change bone length.[3] Surgical limb lengthening by distraction osteogenesis is a distinct procedure that slowly separates cut bone, and it has its own complication rates.[2]

chain: Spine pulled or decompressed in the device
Intervertebral discs rehydrate and posture loosens
Slightly taller measured height for a while
angle.text: The device temporarily lengthens the spinal column by a small amount, so the person measures taller for a period. Because discs compress again during the day, the gain is short-term.

paras: Measured height varies over a day, with exercise before measuring lowering it and lying down raising it.[3] Age-related height loss is partly due to drying of the discs.[3]
Stretching machines load the spine in a way that is meant to separate vertebrae and let discs take on fluid, which is the same physiology behind morning-versus-evening differences.

Height forums discuss stretching, hanging and traction along with posture, shoes and insoles, and bonesmashing as ways to look taller. Threads about height increase after adolescence typically ask whether gains are real growth or posture improvement.[4]

Distraction osteogenesis cuts a bone and separates the ends at around 1 mm per day while new bone forms; complication rates reported include infection of about 5% and bone growing in the wrong direction in 7-9%.[2] Cosmetic limb lengthening has been in demand in India, and China's Ministry of Health banned it in 2006 after serious side effects.[2]

No studies found on commercial stretching machines for height. A 2018 randomised trial in Applied Ergonomics examined propped slouched sitting postures as ways to rehydrate discs and increase spinal height.[1]

refs.title: Increased spinal height using propped slouched sitting postures: Innovative ways to rehydrate intervertebral discs
